title: Greedy Algorithms
tagline: The technique that builds a globally optimal solution by always making the locally best choice at each step — when it works, it works blazingly fast.

sections.content:
There is a class of algorithm that feels almost too simple to be correct: look at all your options right now, pick the best-looking one, commit to it forever, and never look back. No table of subproblem answers, no recursive exploration of every branch — just a single confident choice at each step. This is the **greedy paradigm**, and when it applies, it is one of the most powerful tools in a programmer's toolkit.

A **greedy algorithm** constructs a solution incrementally, always making the locally optimal choice at the current decision point with the expectation — and, when provable, the guarantee — that those local choices accumulate into a globally optimal solution. The word 'greedy' captures the character of the approach: the algorithm does not save anything for later, does not hedge its bets, and does not reconsider. It grabs the best available option immediately and moves on.

This makes greedy algorithms extraordinarily fast in practice. Where dynamic programming might fill an O(n²) or O(n·W) table, greedy typically achieves O(n log n) (dominated by a sort) or even O(n) (a single pass). The catch — and it is a serious one — is that greedy does not work for every problem. Knowing *when* to trust a greedy approach, and *how to prove* that trust is warranted, is the core skill this chapter builds.

The two structural conditions that guarantee correctness are the **greedy choice property** (there always exists an optimal solution that includes the current greedy choice, so committing to it cannot cut off the optimal path) and **optimal substructure** (once the greedy choice is made, the remaining subproblem also has an optimal structure that greedy can exploit). We will examine these conditions carefully, see them at work in four classical algorithms — activity selection, Huffman encoding, fractional knapsack, and Dijkstra's shortest path — and understand precisely why they fail for 0/1 knapsack and arbitrary-denomination coin change.

flowchart LR
    A["All candidates"] --> B["Select best candidate\n(greedy criterion)"]
    B --> C{"Feasible?"}
    C -- "Yes" --> D["Add to solution"]
    C -- "No" --> E["Discard"]

sections.caption: Generic greedy template: at each step, select the best remaining candidate by your greedy criterion, test feasibility, commit or discard, and repeat until done. The algorithm never revisits a discarded or committed choice.

sections.title: Booking the Taxi Fleet With the Shortest Rides First
sections.content:
Imagine you manage a single taxi and a queue of ride requests, each with a pickup time and a drop-off time. You want to fit as many rides into the day as possible — revenue per ride does not matter, only count. You cannot split a ride or overlap two.

Intuitively you might try to pick the shortest rides, thinking short rides free the taxi quickly. But 'shortest duration' is not the right greedy criterion — a short ride starting late still blocks a long run of earlier rides. The correct criterion is **earliest drop-off time**: always choose the ride that finishes soonest among those you haven't started yet. Why? Once that ride ends, the taxi becomes free at the earliest possible moment for the next ride. By continually freeing the taxi as early as possible, you maximise the room for future rides.

This is the **Activity Selection Problem**, the canonical greedy success story. The insight — 'minimise the time you are committed' — has an exact mathematical counterpart called the **exchange argument**, which we will meet shortly. The remarkable thing is that this greedy strategy produces the absolute maximum number of non-overlapping rides, and you can prove it without ever examining all possible subsets.

Greedy algorithms all have this flavour: find the right criterion (one that 'keeps options open' or 'minimises future cost'), commit greedily, and prove by exchange argument that the commitment is always safe.

sections.title: The Two Structural Conditions for Greedy Correctness
sections.content:
Before you reach for a greedy algorithm, you need to verify two properties. Both are necessary; either alone is insufficient.

**1. Greedy Choice Property**

A globally optimal solution can always be constructed so that the first choice is the greedy choice. More precisely: there exists at least one optimal solution that begins with the greedy selection. This does not mean every greedy choice leads to an optimal solution — it means you can always *find* an optimal solution by starting with the greedy pick.

The standard proof technique is the **exchange argument**. Suppose OPT is an optimal solution that does *not* start with the greedy choice G. Show that you can replace whatever OPT starts with by G, producing a solution OPT' that is at least as good as OPT. If this swap never hurts, then G is safe to commit to, and the greedy choice property holds.

For activity selection: OPT begins with activity X (not the earliest-ending one G). Swap X for G. G ends no later than X (by definition of greedy choice), so all subsequent activities that were compatible with X are still compatible after the swap. OPT' has the same number of activities — it is also optimal. Swap is safe. QED.

**2. Optimal Substructure**

After making the greedy choice and removing it from the problem, the remaining subproblem has the same structure and can also be solved optimally by greedy. This is the same property dynamic programming exploits, but greedy uses it differently: rather than solving all subproblems and combining, greedy commits to one choice and recurses into only the one remaining subproblem.

Together these properties mean: greedy's first choice is always in *some* optimal solution, and the subproblem that remains is itself amenable to greedy. By induction, the full greedy solution is optimal.

sections.title: Activity Selection: The Canonical Greedy Algorithm
sections.content:
**Problem statement**: Given n activities, each with a start time sᵢ and finish time fᵢ (sᵢ < fᵢ), select the maximum number of mutually non-overlapping activities. Two activities overlap if and only if one starts before the other ends.

**Greedy strategy**: Sort all activities by finish time (ascending). Scan left to right; greedily select an activity if its start time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the last selected activity.

**Why it works**: After sorting, the algorithm maintains one invariant: `lastEnd` is the earliest possible finish time for any valid selection made so far. When we pick the next compatible activity (one whose start is ≥ `lastEnd`), we again advance `lastEnd` to the earliest possible value. Every step minimises how far into the future we are committed, maximising the window available for subsequent activities.

**Time complexity**: O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the scan — total O(n log n). If the input arrives pre-sorted (a common case in real systems), the algorithm is O(n) — a single pass.

**Space complexity**: O(n) for the result list; O(1) additional working space beyond the input.

**Edge cases to consider**:
- Ties on finish time: any tie-breaking rule works — the exchange argument holds regardless.
- Activities with identical start and end times (zero duration): treated as non-overlapping with everything, so they all get selected.
- A single activity: trivially selected.
- All activities overlapping with each other: only one is selected (whichever finishes earliest).

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The activity selection function sorts once (O(n log n)) and makes a single linear pass maintaining `lastEnd`. The greedy invariant is that after each selection, `lastEnd` equals the minimum possible endpoint for any valid partial schedule of the same size. The coin change example illustrates the failure mode: greedy works for US denominations (each coin is a multiple of all smaller ones — a property called 'canonical'), but fails for arbitrary systems where large coins can block better combinations.

sections.title: Huffman Encoding: Greedy Optimal Compression
sections.content:
**Problem**: Assign a binary code to each symbol in an alphabet so that (a) no code is a prefix of another (prefix-free, enabling unambiguous decoding) and (b) the total number of bits needed to encode a given message is minimised. Symbols that appear more frequently should get shorter codes.

**Why this is a greedy problem**: The optimal prefix-free code can be represented as a binary tree where each leaf is a symbol and the code for that symbol is the path from root to leaf (0 for left, 1 for right). The total encoding cost is the sum of (frequency × depth) across all leaves. To minimise this, frequent symbols should be shallow and infrequent symbols deep — the rarest symbols should be deepest, and the rarest pair should be siblings at the deepest level.

**Greedy strategy — the Huffman algorithm** (David Huffman, 1952):
1. Insert all symbols as leaf nodes into a **min-heap** (priority queue), keyed by frequency.
2. While the heap has more than one node: extract the two lowest-frequency nodes, create a new internal node whose frequency is their sum, and insert the new node back into the heap.
3. The single remaining node is the root of the Huffman tree. Read codes by tracing paths: left = '0', right = '1'.

**Exchange argument for Huffman**: In any optimal prefix-free tree, the two rarest symbols must be siblings at the maximum depth. Proof by contradiction: if they are not, then some pair of siblings at maximum depth have frequencies no less than our two rarest. Swapping the rarest symbols into those deepest sibling positions decreases (or does not change) total cost — contradicting optimality. Therefore, the greedy choice of merging the two rarest symbols is always in some optimal tree.

**Time complexity**: The heap supports extract-min in O(log n) and insert in O(log n). We perform n−1 merges, each involving two extractions and one insertion: O(n log n) total. With n symbols initially inserted: O(n log n) overall.

**Real-world use**: Huffman coding is the foundation of DEFLATE (used in gzip and ZIP), JPEG and PNG compression, and MP3 audio encoding. It is also used in fax machines and the old PKZIP format. Whenever you see a `.gz` or `.zip` file, Huffman trees are doing part of the work.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A["Frequencies: a=45 b=13 c=12 d=16 e=9 f=5"]
    A --> B["Step 1: merge f=5 + e=9 -> fe=14"]
    B --> C["Step 2: merge b=13 + c=12 -> bc=25"]
    C --> D["Step 3: merge fe=14 + d=16 -> fed=30"]
    D --> E["Step 4: merge bc=25 + fed=30 -> bcfed=55"]
    E --> F["Step 5: merge a=45 + bcfed=55 -> root=100"]
    F --> G["Codes: a=0  b=101  c=100  d=111  e=1101  f=1100"]
sections.caption: Huffman construction: the two lowest-frequency nodes are merged at every step. After 5 merges for 6 symbols, the tree is complete. Frequent symbol 'a' (45%) gets a 1-bit code; rare 'f' (5%) gets 4 bits — minimising total encoded length.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The algorithm uses the min-heap to always access the two lowest-frequency nodes in O(log n). After n-1 merges (for n initial symbols), the tree is complete. The `getCodes` function does a DFS, appending '0' for left and '1' for right at each step. The total bits calculation shows the practical saving: Huffman uses 224 bits vs 300 for fixed-width coding — a 25% reduction even on this small example.

sections.title: Fractional Knapsack vs 0/1 Knapsack: Where Greedy Draws the Line
sections.content:
**The fractional knapsack problem**: You have a knapsack of capacity W and n items, each with a value vᵢ and weight wᵢ. You may take any fraction of an item. Maximise total value without exceeding capacity.

**Greedy strategy**: Compute the value-to-weight ratio rᵢ = vᵢ/wᵢ for each item. Sort by ratio descending. Greedily fill the knapsack with items in ratio order, taking full items until one would overflow — then take the fraction that fills the remaining capacity.

**Why it works**: The exchange argument: in any optimal solution that does not start with the highest-ratio item, we can swap equal weight of the highest-ratio item in for whatever is there. Since rᵢ is maximum, this swap increases or maintains total value. Fractional items make this swap always possible — we can always take exactly the right weight. The greedy choice property holds.

**The 0/1 knapsack problem**: Same setup, but items cannot be split — you take all of an item or none of it. The same greedy strategy by ratio fails. Classic counterexample: capacity 50, items [(value=60, weight=10), (value=100, weight=20), (value=120, weight=30)]. Ratios: 6, 5, 4. Greedy takes item 1 (full, weight 10), item 2 (full, weight 20), then item 3 would fill (weight 30 = 20 remaining... wait, 10+20=30 used, 20 left). Actually greedy takes all three for 280 — this example passes. Use instead: capacity 50, items [(value=60, weight=10), (value=100, weight=40)]. Ratio: 6 vs 2.5. Greedy takes item 1 (60, weight 10), then item 2 doesn't fit fully (40 > 40 remaining)... well, fractional: takes 40/40 of item 2 = 100. Total: 160. But in 0/1 mode: take only item 2 = 100, or only item 1 = 60, or both if they fit (they do: 50 total) = 160. Here they tie, so try: capacity 10, items [(value=60, weight=10), (value=40, weight=5), (value=30, weight=5)]. Ratios: 6, 8, 6. Greedy by ratio: takes item 2 (40, weight 5), item 1 (60, weight 10 — won't fit, 5 remaining), item 3 (30, weight 5 = fits). Total 40+30 = 70. Optimal: item 2 + item 3 = 70. Same here. The classic failure: capacity 6, items [(value=6, weight=6), (value=5, weight=5), (value=4, weight=4)]. Greedy by value/weight: all have ratio 1. Take item 1 (weight 6) = value 6. Optimal: item 2 + item 3 (weight 9 — doesn't fit). So actually: only one item fits. This illustrates that for 0/1 knapsack you cannot simply split to fill gaps — the constraint that items are atomic means past choices can leave wasted capacity that prevents better combinations, and dynamic programming is required.

**Rule of thumb**: If items can be fractioned, greedy by value/weight ratio is optimal. If items are atomic (0 or 1), use DP with table dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w.

sections.caption: The fractional vs 0/1 knapsack split: the ability to take fractions is exactly what enables the exchange argument. Without it, greedy fails and DP is required.

sections.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path: Greedy on a Graph
sections.content:
**Problem**: Given a weighted directed graph with non-negative edge weights, find the shortest path from a source vertex s to all other vertices.

**Greedy strategy (Dijkstra's algorithm, 1956)**: Maintain a set of 'settled' vertices whose shortest distance from s is finalised. At each step, greedily select the unsettled vertex with the current minimum estimated distance, settle it, and update (relax) the distances of its unsettled neighbours.

**Why it works**: The greedy choice property here is: once a vertex is selected as the minimum-distance unsettled vertex, its distance is final. Why? All edge weights are non-negative, so any alternative path to this vertex through an unsettled vertex would have to traverse at least one more non-negative edge — it cannot be shorter. This is the key reason Dijkstra fails on negative edges: a negative edge could allow an unsettled vertex to provide a shorter path than what we finalised.

**Time complexity**: With a binary heap (priority queue), each extract-min is O(log V) and each relaxation (edge update) is O(log V). Total: O((V + E) log V) where V is vertices and E is edges. With a Fibonacci heap this improves to O(E + V log V), but in practice binary heap implementations are faster due to cache effects.

**The greedy character**: Dijkstra is often not called a 'greedy algorithm' in introductory courses, but it perfectly fits the template — select the locally best-looking vertex (minimum distance so far), commit to it, never revisit. The same greedy insight underlies Prim's algorithm for minimum spanning trees (select the minimum-weight edge connecting the tree to a new vertex).

**When Dijkstra breaks**: Negative edge weights violate the greedy choice property — a settled vertex's distance might later be improved via a negative edge. The fix is Bellman-Ford, which runs O(VE) by relaxing all edges V−1 times. For graphs with negative edges, greedy is not applicable and a full DP-style approach is needed.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Source s\ndist=0"]
    A -- "4" --> B["B\ndist=4"]
    A -- "2" --> C["C\ndist=2"]
    C -- "1" --> B
    B -- "3" --> D["D\ndist=7"]
    C -- "5" --> D
sections.caption: Dijkstra trace: from s, settle C (dist 2) first. Relaxing C->B updates B from 4 to 3 (2+1). Settle B (dist 3). Relax B->D: dist 6 (3+3). Settle D (dist 6) — greedy selection of minimum-distance vertex at each step.

sections.title: Proving Greedy Fails: The Counterexample Method
sections.content:
When you suspect greedy might not work for a problem, the fastest proof is a **counterexample** — a small input where greedy gives a suboptimal answer.

**Coin change with [1, 3, 4], target 6**:
- Greedy picks 4 (largest coin ≤ 6), remaining = 2
- Greedy picks 1 (largest coin ≤ 2), remaining = 1
- Greedy picks 1, remaining = 0
- Total: 3 coins
- Optimal: 3 + 3 = 2 coins
- Greedy fails. The greedy choice property does not hold: choosing 4 first means no 3-coin combination is possible for the remainder 2.

**Why canonical denominations work**: US coins [1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100] have a special property — each coin value is a multiple of the previous. This is called a **canonical coin system**, and for canonical systems, the exchange argument for greedy coin change can be proved. For arbitrary denominations, you need DP.

**The general counterexample construction technique**: To disprove a greedy criterion, try small inputs (3-6 elements) where the greedy order differs from the optimal order. Focus on cases where two candidates have similar greedy values but very different downstream effects. If you cannot find a counterexample on small inputs and the exchange argument seems to hold, you likely have a correct greedy algorithm — but you still need to prove it formally for production use.

**Common false greedy approaches**:
- Activity selection by **shortest duration**: fails when a short activity in the middle blocks two activities on either side.
- Activity selection by **earliest start time**: fails when an early-starting activity is very long.
- Knapsack by **highest value**: ignores weight, wastes capacity.
- Graph shortest path by **fewest hops**: ignores edge weights, produces wrong distances.

sections.title: Greedy vs Dynamic Programming: Choosing the Right Tool
sections.content:
Both greedy algorithms and dynamic programming exploit **optimal substructure** — the optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems. The difference is in *how many* subproblems are considered.

**Dynamic programming** solves all subproblems and combines their solutions. It is safe for a wider class of problems because it considers every possibility. The cost is the table: O(n²) or O(n·W) time and space is typical.

**Greedy** commits to one subproblem at each step (the one reached by the greedy choice). It is faster — O(n log n) is common — but requires the stronger **greedy choice property**: the greedy choice is always in some optimal solution.

**Decision tree for problem solving**:
1. Can you identify a greedy criterion (sort by X, always pick the minimum/maximum Y)?
2. Can you prove the greedy choice property via exchange argument?
3. Is optimal substructure easy to see for the remaining subproblem?

If all three hold — greedy. If optimal substructure holds but greedy choice property is unclear or fails — DP. If neither holds — brute force, approximation, or problem-specific techniques.

**Practical performance comparison** (for activity selection as example):
- Greedy: O(n log n) sort + O(n) scan = O(n log n) time, O(n) space
- DP (if formulated as interval scheduling DP): O(n²) time, O(n) space

Greedy wins decisively when it is correct. The interview skill is recognising which regime you are in — and being able to articulate *why* greedy is or is not safe for the specific problem at hand.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The fractional knapsack solution sorts by ratio in O(n log n) and takes a single pass. The key is `Math.min(item.weight, remaining)` — if the best-ratio item fits entirely, take it all; otherwise take only the fraction that fills remaining capacity exactly. The inline checklist at the bottom is a practical protocol for determining whether greedy is safe for any problem you encounter.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Misconception 1: 'Greedy is just an approximation.'** Not true. For problems with both the greedy choice property and optimal substructure, greedy produces a provably optimal solution. Activity selection, Huffman coding, fractional knapsack, Dijkstra, Prim, and Kruskal are all exact, not approximate.

**Misconception 2: 'If greedy looks right on examples, it is correct.'** Small examples can be deceiving. Greedy coin change looks right for [1, 5, 10, 25] on many test cases before you try [1, 3, 4] with target 6. Always seek a formal proof or a counterexample.

**Misconception 3: 'Greedy and DP are mutually exclusive.'** Some algorithms combine both. Dijkstra, for example, uses a greedy selection rule (pick minimum distance vertex) but relaxes all outgoing edges — the relaxation step is a form of optimal substructure exploitation. The two paradigms are complementary, not competing.

**Misconception 4: 'Earliest start time works for activity selection.'** It does not. Consider activities [(0, 100), (1, 2), (3, 4)]: earliest-start picks (0, 100), then cannot pick anything (both others end before 100). Maximum is 2 activities: (1,2) and (3,4). Earliest finish time correctly selects those two.

**Edge case: duplicate finish times in activity selection.** When two activities end at the same time, either one can be selected — the exchange argument shows both choices lead to equally optimal results. Any tie-breaking rule is valid.

**Edge case: empty input.** Always check n = 0 or n = 1 — the base cases where 'sort by criterion' and 'merge the two smallest' need guard clauses.

**Edge case: all identical frequencies in Huffman.** If all symbols have equal frequency, the Huffman tree is not unique — many balanced trees are all optimal. The algorithm will still produce one valid optimal tree.

sections.title: Real-World Applications and Historical Context
sections.content:
Greedy algorithms are not academic curiosities — they power critical infrastructure.

**Data compression**: Huffman coding (1952) is the basis of DEFLATE, used in gzip, ZIP, PNG, and HTTP content-encoding. Modern compression formats like LZ77 and LZ78 (which underlie gzip's full algorithm) use Huffman as a final entropy-coding stage. Even JPEG uses Huffman coding for its entropy-coding step.

**Network routing**: Dijkstra's shortest path (1956, published 1959) underlies OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), the interior gateway routing protocol used throughout the internet. Every packet your browser sends is routed by algorithms descended from Dijkstra's greedy insight.

**Minimum spanning trees**: Kruskal's (1956) and Prim's (1957) algorithms — both greedy — find minimum spanning trees and are used in network design, circuit board layout, and approximation algorithms for the traveling salesman problem.

**Scheduling in operating systems**: CPU schedulers use greedy-flavoured algorithms. Shortest Job First (SJF) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF, used in real-time systems) are greedy approaches to minimising average wait time or meeting deadline constraints.

**Caching and memory management**: The **greedy algorithm for optimal caching** (Belady's algorithm) is theoretically optimal: when the cache is full, evict the page that will be used furthest in the future. In practice, since we cannot see the future, LRU (Least Recently Used) is the greedy approximation — evict what has not been used longest, as a proxy for 'least likely needed soon'.

**The history of the word 'greedy' in algorithms** traces to operations research and the work of Edmonds (1971), who formally characterised the class of problems for which greedy succeeds — the theory of **matroids**. A matroid is an abstract combinatorial structure that precisely captures the greedy choice property. Activity selection, Huffman, and spanning trees all correspond to matroid optimisation problems.

**Matroids and the deep theory of greedy**: Edmonds (1971) proved that greedy produces an optimal solution if and only if the problem's feasibility structure is a **matroid** — an abstract structure that generalises the notion of 'independent sets' in linear algebra. Activity selection (choosing non-overlapping activities), spanning trees (choosing acyclic edge sets), and Huffman (choosing prefix-free code sets) are all matroid problems. If you can show your problem's feasible sets form a matroid (closed under subsets, augmentation property holds), you immediately know greedy is optimal. This connection explains *why* greedy works on a deep mathematical level, beyond case-by-case exchange arguments.

**Interview and exam insights for greedy problems**:

- **Recognise the pattern**: Greedy problems almost always involve sorting by some criterion first, then a single pass. If you find yourself sorting by X and scanning linearly, you are probably doing greedy.
- **State the greedy criterion explicitly**: In an interview, say 'I will always pick the activity with the earliest finish time because...' before coding. Examiners want to see that you understand *why*, not just that you know the algorithm.
- **Prove correctness with an exchange argument** (even verbally): 'If OPT does not start with our greedy choice, we can swap in our choice without making OPT worse — here is why.' This one sentence distinguishes a strong candidate.
- **Common greedy interview problems**: interval scheduling/merging, task scheduling with deadlines, minimum number of platforms (equivalent to activity selection), jump game, gas station, candy distribution.
- **Watch for the coin-change trap**: If the problem says 'minimum number of coins/items/operations' and the denomination/item set is arbitrary — it is DP, not greedy. Only attempt greedy for coin change if the problem explicitly states canonical denominations or asks you to prove it works.
- **Dijkstra requires non-negative weights**: If the problem has negative edge weights, state that Dijkstra does not apply and switch to Bellman-Ford.

items: A **greedy algorithm** makes the locally optimal choice at each step and never backtracks. It is correct only when the problem has both the **greedy choice property** (the local choice is always part of some optimal global solution) and **optimal substructure** (the remaining subproblem is also optimally solvable by greedy).

The **exchange argument** is the standard proof of the greedy choice property: assume an optimal solution that differs from greedy at the first step, swap in the greedy choice, and show the result is no worse. If the swap is always safe, greedy is correct.

**Activity selection** (always pick earliest finish time) achieves maximum non-overlapping intervals in O(n log n) — a single sort followed by a linear scan. Sorting by duration or start time gives wrong answers.

**Huffman encoding** greedily merges the two lowest-frequency symbols using a min-heap, producing the minimum expected-length prefix-free code in O(n log n). It is the basis of DEFLATE, gzip, ZIP, PNG, and JPEG entropy coding.

**Fractional knapsack** (sort by value/weight ratio, fill greedily) is solvable by greedy because fractions allow the exchange argument to hold. **0/1 knapsack** (no splitting) requires DP with an O(n·W) table — greedy fails because atomic items can leave wasted capacity.

**Dijkstra's shortest path** is a greedy algorithm on graphs: always settle the unsettled vertex with minimum current distance. It requires **non-negative edge weights** — the greedy choice property breaks on negative edges (use Bellman-Ford instead).

When in doubt, **try a counterexample on 3–5 elements**: find a small input where greedy picks a different order than optimal. If a counterexample exists, use DP. If you cannot find one and the exchange argument holds, greedy is likely correct — but prove it formally.

quiz.question: Which two structural properties must a problem satisfy for a greedy algorithm to guarantee a globally optimal solution?
options: Overlapping subproblems and memoisation compatibility
Greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Sorted input and divide-and-conquer decomposition
Polynomial time complexity and linear space requirement
quiz.explanation: The greedy choice property guarantees that the local greedy selection is always part of some globally optimal solution (proved by exchange argument). Optimal substructure guarantees that the remaining subproblem after the greedy choice is also optimally solvable. Both are necessary — either alone is insufficient to guarantee correctness.

quiz.question: In the activity selection problem, the correct greedy criterion is to always pick the activity with the:
options: Earliest start time
Shortest duration
Earliest finish time
Highest start time
quiz.explanation: Earliest finish time is the correct greedy criterion. It minimises how far into the future the resource is committed after each selection, maximising the window available for future activities. Earliest start time and shortest duration both fail — counterexamples exist for each.

quiz.question: What is an 'exchange argument' in the context of proving a greedy algorithm correct?
options: Swapping two elements in an array to sort it in-place
Assuming an optimal solution that diverges from greedy, swapping in the greedy choice, and showing the result is no worse
Replacing the greedy algorithm with dynamic programming when greedy fails
Comparing greedy output against brute-force output on random inputs
quiz.explanation: The exchange argument is the canonical technique for proving the greedy choice property. You take any optimal solution that first diverges from the greedy solution, replace that first differing choice with the greedy choice, and demonstrate the modified solution is still optimal (or better). If this holds universally, the greedy choice is always safe to make.

quiz.question: Why does greedy coin change fail for denominations [1, 3, 4] with target amount 6?
options: Greedy cannot handle coin values larger than the target divided by 2
Greedy picks 4 then uses two 1s (3 coins), missing the optimal 3+3 (2 coins)
The algorithm does not terminate because 6 is not divisible by any denomination
Greedy fails whenever the denomination set does not include 2
quiz.explanation: Greedy takes the largest coin not exceeding the remaining amount: 4 (remaining 2), then 1 (remaining 1), then 1 (done) — 3 coins. The optimal solution is 3+3 = 2 coins. The greedy choice property fails: committing to coin 4 prevents reaching the better 3+3 combination.

quiz.question: Huffman encoding builds the optimal prefix-free code tree by repeatedly:
options: Splitting the highest-frequency symbol into two child nodes
Merging the two lowest-frequency nodes into a single parent node using a min-heap
Assigning bit codes based on alphabetical order of symbols
Balancing the tree so all leaves are at the same depth
quiz.explanation: Huffman's algorithm uses a min-heap to always extract the two lowest-frequency nodes, merges them into a parent node with frequency equal to their sum, and reinserts the parent. After n-1 such merges (for n symbols), the single remaining node is the root. Rare symbols naturally end up deepest, getting the longest codes.

quiz.question: Which of the following problems is correctly solved by a greedy algorithm?
options: 0/1 Knapsack with arbitrary integer weights and values
Coin change with arbitrary denominations to minimise coin count
Fractional Knapsack — items may be taken in any fraction
Longest increasing subsequence in an unsorted array
quiz.explanation: Fractional Knapsack allows splitting items, so sorting by value/weight ratio and greedily filling holds an exchange argument: any alternative use of the same weight from a lower-ratio item can be swapped for the highest-ratio item without decreasing value. 0/1 knapsack, arbitrary coin change, and LIS all require dynamic programming.

quiz.question: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm fails on graphs with negative edge weights because:
options: The min-heap cannot store negative values
A settled vertex's distance might later be improved via a negative edge, violating the greedy choice property
Negative edges create cycles that cause the algorithm to loop forever
The algorithm's time complexity becomes exponential with negative weights
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy choice property relies on the fact that, for non-negative weights, the minimum-distance unsettled vertex cannot be further improved by any path through other unsettled vertices. A negative edge breaks this guarantee — a later vertex could offer a shortcut. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing all edges V-1 times instead of making greedy selections.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of Huffman encoding using a proper binary min-heap?
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
quiz.explanation: With n initial symbols, Huffman performs n-1 merges. Each merge involves two extract-min operations (O(log n) each) and one insert (O(log n)). Total: O(n log n). If a sorted array is rebuilt after each merge, the complexity degrades to O(n²). A min-heap is the standard efficient implementation.

quiz.question: For the activity selection problem with n activities, what is the time complexity of the greedy algorithm?
options: O(n) always
O(n log n) due to sorting, O(n) if already sorted
O(n²) due to pairwise overlap checking
O(n log² n)
quiz.explanation: The dominant cost is sorting activities by finish time: O(n log n). After sorting, a single linear scan (O(n)) selects activities greedily. Total: O(n log n). If the input arrives pre-sorted by finish time (a common scenario in calendar/scheduling systems), the sort is skipped and the algorithm runs in O(n).

quiz.question: You have items with values and weights, a knapsack capacity W, and each item can be taken at most once (no splitting). You want to maximise total value. Which approach is correct?
options: Greedy: sort by value/weight ratio descending, fill greedily
Dynamic programming: dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w, O(n*W)
Greedy: sort by value descending, take items until full
Either greedy or DP — they produce identical results for integer weights
quiz.explanation: This is 0/1 Knapsack. Items cannot be split, so the greedy exchange argument breaks: taking a high-ratio item may leave capacity that cannot be filled efficiently by remaining items. DP with table dp[i][w] correctly handles all combinations. The space-optimised 1D DP variant reduces space to O(W) while keeping time at O(n*W).
